explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Paul says that if the earthly tent is dismantled, "we have a building from God, an eternal house in heaven, not built by human hands." (2 Corinthians 5:1) A tent is a temporary place to stay, and this house is the opposite. It comes from God, and it doesn't pack up.

I get why you'd pick it, friend. A tougher tent sounds nice, especially when mine has been through a lot of batches. But Paul doesn't say God hands us an upgraded tent. He says we have "a building from God, an eternal house in heaven." (2 Corinthians 5:1)

explanations.answer: A longer stay in this tent
explanations.explanation: Nope, no extension on the tent rental here, baker. Paul says that when the tent is dismantled, we have "a building from God, an eternal house in heaven, not built by human hands." (2 Corinthians 5:1) So it's a whole different kind of home, not more time in the old one.

Careful, friend, this one is a trick. Paul says the opposite. He calls it "an eternal house in heaven, not built by human hands." (2 Corinthians 5:1) No contractor, no crew, and no hammer anyone here has ever held.

Right, baker. Paul says the house is "a building from God, an eternal house in heaven, not built by human hands." (2 Corinthians 5:1) Human hands didn't build it, so no human hands can wear it out either. I think that's good news for anybody who has ever lived with a leaky roof.

explanations.answer: To be clothed with our heavenly dwelling
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Paul says, "in this tent we groan, longing to be clothed with our heavenly dwelling." (2 Corinthians 5:2) The groaning isn't random. It points toward something we're longing for. Paul pictures that dwelling as something we put on, like clothes.

explanations.answer: To keep living in this earthly tent
explanations.explanation: Close, friend, but that's not what Paul says. The longing he names is "to be clothed with our heavenly dwelling." (2 Corinthians 5:2) The tent is where we groan, not what we're longing for. Even a stamper who loves his bakery can tell the difference.

explanations.answer: To forget the troubles of this life
explanations.explanation: I see why that sounds right, baker, since groaning and troubles go together. But Paul never says we long to forget anything. He says we're "longing to be clothed with our heavenly dwelling." (2 Corinthians 5:2) The longing points toward something, not away from something.

That's it, baker. Paul says, "when we are clothed, we will not be found naked." (2 Corinthians 5:3) He's using the picture of clothing for the heavenly dwelling. Once we're clothed, we won't be found without it.

That's a sweet thought, friend, but it's not the word Paul uses. He says, "when we are clothed, we will not be found naked." (2 Corinthians 5:3) The picture is about clothing, so the word he picks fits the picture.

Good guess, baker, because being found and being lost go together like dough and a hot oven. But Paul's word is a different one. He says, "when we are clothed, we will not be found naked." (2 Corinthians 5:3)
That's right, baker. Paul says, "we groan under our burdens, because we do not wish to be unclothed but clothed." (2 Corinthians 5:4) The wish is to be clothed, and the burdens are why he's groaning.
This one fooled me for a second, friend. Paul really does say it: "we do not wish to be unclothed but clothed." (2 Corinthians 5:4) So the statement is true, and the wish is to be clothed.

Yes, baker, life. Paul says we wish to be clothed "so that our mortality may be swallowed up by life." (2 Corinthians 5:4) Notice what's doing the swallowing. It's life, and mortality is what gets swallowed.
Time is a good guess, friend, since it's always running out in my bakery. But Paul's word is different. He says "so that our mortality may be swallowed up by life." (2 Corinthians 5:4)

I can see why sorrow came to mind, baker, with all that groaning going around. But Paul doesn't say sorrow. He says "so that our mortality may be swallowed up by life." (2 Corinthians 5:4) Life is what does the swallowing.

That's the one, baker. Paul says God "has given us the Spirit as a pledge of what is to come." (2 Corinthians 5:5) A pledge is a promise you can hold onto. So the Spirit is how God backs up what's coming.
An angel would be impressive, I'll admit, friend. I've met one, and I still think about it. But Paul says God "has given us the Spirit as a pledge of what is to come." (2 Corinthians 5:5)

Ha, my favorite color made the list, baker. A rainbow does show up as God's sign in Genesis 9:13, but that's a different promise. Here Paul says God "has given us the Spirit as a pledge of what is to come." (2 Corinthians 5:5)

Yes, baker. Paul says, "we are always confident, although we know that while we are at home in the body, we are away from the Lord." (2 Corinthians 5:6) Both things are true at once. Away from the Lord for now, and still confident.

I get the hesitation, friend. Being away from the Lord sounds like a reason to worry. But Paul says, "we are always confident, although we know that while we are at home in the body, we are away from the Lord." (2 Corinthians 5:6) So the statement is true.

explanations.answer: By faith and not by sight
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Paul says, "we walk by faith, not by sight." (2 Corinthians 5:7) We can't see the Lord right now, so we go on trusting. Faith is how we get through the day.

explanations.answer: By sight and not by faith
explanations.explanation: That's the flip, friend, and Paul flips it right back. He says, "we walk by faith, not by sight." (2 Corinthians 5:7) If we only walked by what we could see, I'd still be sitting in that drawer.

Nice try, baker, but Paul doesn't say that. He says, "we walk by faith, not by sight." (2 Corinthians 5:7) And he's already told us it's God who prepared us and gave us the Spirit as a pledge (2 Corinthians 5:5), so we're not on our own.
Yes, baker, prefer. Paul says, "We are confident, then, and would prefer to be away from the body and at home with the Lord." (2 Corinthians 5:8) Being at home with the Lord is what he'd choose.

That's the opposite direction, friend. Paul says, "We are confident, then, and would prefer to be away from the body and at home with the Lord." (2 Corinthians 5:8) Nothing about refusing there. He's looking forward to being at home with the Lord.

I see why dread came to mind, baker, since nobody loves thinking about leaving the body. But Paul says the opposite. "We are confident, then, and would prefer to be away from the body and at home with the Lord." (2 Corinthians 5:8)

That's right, baker. Paul says, "we aspire to please Him, whether we are at home in this body or away from it." (2 Corinthians 5:9) The aim doesn't change with the address. At home in the body or away from it, the goal stays the same.

Rest sounds lovely, friend, especially after a full day of stamping. But Paul doesn't say that here. He says, "we aspire to please Him, whether we are at home in this body or away from it." (2 Corinthians 5:9)
A little applause is nice, baker, I won't lie. But that's not Paul's aim here. He says, "we aspire to please Him, whether we are at home in this body or away from it." (2 Corinthians 5:9)

explanations.answer: Before the judgment seat of Christ
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Paul says, "we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ." (2 Corinthians 5:10) Notice the word "all." It includes every one of us, Paul too.
That's a real place in the Bible, friend, but not the one Paul names here. He says, "we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ." (2 Corinthians 5:10)

Good thinking, baker, since a judgment seat could sound like a Roman thing. Caesar was the Roman emperor, and Paul once appealed to him (Acts 25:11). But here Paul says, "we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ." (2 Corinthians 5:10)
Not quite, baker. Paul says each one receives "his due for the things done in the body, whether good or bad." (2 Corinthians 5:10) So the text doesn't limit it to the good things only.

Right, baker. Paul says we appear "that each one may receive his due for the things done in the body, whether good or bad." (2 Corinthians 5:10) Both good and bad are named, so "only the good" doesn't match the text.
